title: Language Access in Palliative Care: What the Data Shows
summary: Language barriers in palliative care cause consent errors and worse outcomes for LEP patients. See the data and how to close the gaps. July 2026.
body_markdown:
###


Without a trained interpreter, goals-of-care discussions often fail to produce an accurate record of what the patient actually wants. Research shows that patients with language barriers are less likely to change to a do-not-resuscitate code status, not because they want aggressive intervention, but because the conversation needed to confirm their preferences never happened accurately.


###


Opalite Health is designed to support high-stakes clinical conversations, including goals-of-care discussions, as part of a risk-based language access program that defines when AI interpretation is appropriate and when escalation to a qualified human interpreter is required. For the most sensitive encounters, such as complex informed consent or DNR discussions, healthcare organizations set their own escalation policies, and Opalite works within those boundaries and does not replace them.


###


Language barriers slow every step of hospice enrollment: grasping the prognosis, choosing comfort over curative treatment, and completing consent paperwork all require accurate interpretation. One study found that 54% of hospice bereavement coordinators reported needing more interpreter services for patients with limited English proficiency, meaning the gap persists even after the patient has died.


###


A trained professional medical interpreter produces better outcomes than a family member or an untrained phone service. One systematic review found that care quality in end-of-life settings varied by interpreter type across every study reviewed, with untrained family members introducing accuracy problems and ethical conflicts that a professional interpreter avoids.


###


Opalite Health is designed to work alongside qualified human interpreters as part of a broader language access program, not to replace them. For routine and urgent encounters, it provides instant access across more than 150 languages; for the highest-risk conversations, organizations define escalation policies that route patients to a human interpreter when the clinical or consent stakes require it.
